content: In 2017, over 860,000 individuals of Rohingya ethnicity fled Myanmar and settled in refugee camps around Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, which now hosts the largest refugee camp population globally. The National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) was expanded to include these camps and their host communities, in collaboration with the Bangladesh Rural Advancement Committee (BRAC), the World Health Organization (WHO), and other partners such as UNHCR, IOM, Médecins Sans Frontières, and Save the Children. Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis and treatment services were established within the camps and nearby health centers in surrounding sub-districts (upazilas). At the community level, field staff identified and referred suspected TB cases, supported patients during treatment, and provided health education and community engagement. The COVID-19 pandemic began spreading among the refugee and host populations in early 2020. Prior to this, every four months, approximately 130,000 Rohingya refugees and 12,000–15,000 individuals from host communities were screened for TB, with 8,000 and 900–1,100 cases confirmed, respectively. Treatment success rates exceeded 95%. However, the onset of COVID-19 led to movement restrictions, severely limiting TB services, including diagnosis, treatment follow-up, patient support, health education, and community engagement. Stigma associated with both TB and COVID-19, along with fears of quarantine, discouraged individuals from seeking healthcare. Between April and June 2020, only 5,454 Rohingya refugees and 2,087 host community members were screened, with 395 and 273 cases confirmed, respectively. Despite these challenges, staff continued their work, albeit with concerns about treatment outcomes. Laboratory and field staff received additional training on COVID-19 infection control measures. The government and national actors, such as ministries of health and other relevant agencies, play a primary role in initiating, organizing, coordinating, and implementing emergency preparedness and response, including humanitarian assistance and healthcare. Addressing TB prevention and care among refugees and other affected populations requires sustainable, system-supporting interventions led by the health ministry in collaboration with all sectors within the host country. According to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and WHO’s End TB Strategy, governments must act as duty-bearers and stewards while engaging a wide range of stakeholders, including civil society, affected communities, NGOs, and private health providers. Coordination across national ministries, regional and local authorities, and other actors is essential, and understanding local coordination models and past precedents is critical. Nearly every country has an NTP, typically with a central unit and regional or district focal points, though staffing and structure vary depending on the overall health system. In most countries, TB care and prevention are integrated into primary care, community-based care, and other levels of the health system. The quality and coverage of services depend heavily on human and financial resources for healthcare. UNHCR’s work with refugees is a distinct yet integral part of the overall humanitarian coordination framework. It operates throughout refugee responses, whether in new or protracted emergencies, and across various settings, including camps, rural areas, urban environments, or mixed situations. UNHCR leads the development, implementation, and resource mobilization for interagency refugee response plans, which establish a common strategy and provide host governments and donors with an overview of the interagency response, including resource requirements. Additionally, UNHCR assists governments in establishing and supporting national, regional, and international arrangements for applying the Global Compact on Refugees, which emphasizes predictable and equitable responsibility-sharing and recognizes the need for international cooperation to achieve sustainable solutions for refugee situations. Civil society organizations play a vital role in humanitarian emergencies by promoting rights-based approaches, contributing to policies and partnerships, and overseeing implementation. Many international and national NGOs active in humanitarian emergencies also work in health, including TB prevention and care. The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria encourages countries to include refugees and displaced populations in their funding applications to promote sustainability and equity. Countries experiencing humanitarian emergencies may benefit from the Challenging Operating Environments Policy, which allows flexibility in using funds for affected populations and their host communities through reprogramming existing grants or applying for the Emergency Fund. Since 2016, the World Bank has included engagement in situations of fragility, conflict, and violence as part of its strategy to end poverty and promote shared prosperity. This approach involves addressing long-term developmental challenges through early engagement, sustained presence in conflict-affected areas, and continuous dialogue with parties involved in violent conflicts. Addressing the impact of TB on refugees and displaced populations requires the engagement of various non-state and government actors, including those in home and foreign affairs, justice, labor, social affairs, education, and health. Multisectoral, multilevel, and transnational approaches are essential for coordinated, structural, and sustainable change to ensure the health of refugees. Joint policies and interventions must adhere to the principle of non-discrimination and follow a human rights-based approach to ensure accountability. Afghanistan has one of the highest numbers of refugees, returnees, and internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Asia, with 4 million documented Afghan refugees and 2 million IDPs. These populations face higher TB risks due to poor living conditions and limited access to healthcare. In January 2019, a three-year multicountry TB grant from the Global Fund was launched to ensure access to quality TB care for Afghan refugees and migrants. This grant has supported approximately 1 million refugees, returnees, and IDPs across Afghanistan, Iran, and Pakistan. Active case-finding strategies were introduced to address access barriers and screen target populations. New diagnostic tools, such as GeneXpert in Afghanistan, were implemented following comprehensive health facility assessments. In 2020, active case finding screened 983,193 individuals and detected 945 TB cases, achieving 145% of the target for that year. One major success of the multicountry grant was the development and adoption of a sub-regional strategic plan for cross-border TB care and prevention, along with harmonized and updated national guidelines for TB active case finding. These documents were integrated into national strategic plans to ensure consistency and sustainability of TB care and prevention among Afghan migrants. Additionally, a cross-border digital platform is being developed to facilitate TB data sharing among the three countries. Expected to be operational by 2022, this platform aims to improve TB screening, registration, testing, tracking, treatment enrollment, and follow-up, ultimately reducing “lost to follow-up” cases and increasing treatment success rates. Preparedness for humanitarian emergency responses can save time and lives. Emergency management authorities, with the involvement of various ministries, institutions, and partners, typically lead preparedness efforts. The health ministry is usually the primary actor in addressing health risks. While preparedness plans often do not focus on individual disease responses, TB and its drug-resistant forms pose significant public health risks that must be addressed. National TB strategies should include components for emergency planning, complementing overall health plans. Strengthening national TB strategic plans (NSPs) can enable better planning for TB responses in humanitarian emergencies. This chapter provides guidance and tools for specific planning elements that can benefit both national and TB-specific strategic and operational planning.
